notes: Ruling slot 4 = Communist Party of Ukraine under Petro Shelest (MD sprite ukr_cpu is not in md_sprites_for_tag, so icon null). Emigre camps spread by ideology: UHVR/Lebed (0, CIA-backed), UNR State Centre/Livytsky (1), URDP (3), OUN-M (20), OUN-B/Stetsko (21). Shcherbytsky's Council of Ministers in 13, Dnipropetrovsk clan (Vatchenko) in 15, Ukrainian KGB (Nikitchenko) in 7, Malanchuk hardliners in 6. Crimean Tatar movement kept in 12 as MD does with Crimean Tatar organizations. Islamic slots 8, 9, 11 use foreign student circles; 10 the Ufa muftiate. Slot 23 uses MD sprite UKR_monarchism (House of Skoropadsky).

0.name: Ukrayinska Holovna Vyzvolna Rada
0.text:
The Ukrainian Supreme Liberation Council was founded in the Carpathians in 1944 as the political authority of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. Since the insurgency was crushed it survives through its Foreign Representation in New York, led by Mykola Lebed, wartime acting chief of the Bandera wing, and the priest Ivan Hrynioch. Their Prolog publishing house and the Munich monthly Suchasnist, quietly funded by American intelligence, reach Soviet visitors and intellectuals.

The council claims to be the rightful underground authority of an independent Ukraine and works hand in hand with Washington against Moscow. It has shed the one-party creed of integral nationalism for a pragmatic Western course, yet remains a tight conspiracy whose leaders expect to rule by right of the liberation struggle. Its leverage is American money and émigré scholarship.

1.name: Derzhavnyi Tsentr Ukrayinskoyi Narodnoyi Respubliky v ekzyli
1.english: State Centre of the Ukrainian People's Republic in Exile
1.native_full: Derzhavnyi Tsentr Ukrayinskoyi Narodnoyi Respubliky v ekzyli
1.text:
The State Centre of the Ukrainian People's Republic in Exile carries the legal continuity of the republic that Symon Petliura defended until 1920. Its President since 1967 is Mykola Livytsky, son of the earlier exile president Andriy Livytsky, who presides from Munich over an exile government and the Ukrainian National Council, a parliament of émigré parties from Germany, North America and Australia.

It stands for an independent, democratic and Christian Ukraine, a parliamentary republic with private property and a market economy, firmly in the Western camp. It lobbies governments abroad, commemorates the national revolution and the famine of 1933, and rejects both Soviet rule and the authoritarian nationalism of the Bandera wing. Its leverage is legitimacy and the votes of Ukrainian communities in Canada and the United States.

2.name: Shistdesiatnyky
2.text:
The Sixtiers are the generation of Ukrainian poets, critics and artists who came of age in the Khrushchev thaw and refused to accept Russification. After the arrests of 1965 and 1966 they turned to samizdat and open letters. The journalist Vyacheslav Chornovil, whose record of the political trials circulated abroad as The Chornovil Papers, the critic Ivan Svitlychny and the painter Alla Horska are their leading figures in Lviv and Kyiv.

They demand that the Soviet constitution be honoured: free speech, open trials, an end to political imprisonment and equal standing for Ukrainian in schools, universities and publishing. Democratic and humanist rather than revolutionary, they look to European culture and the Moscow rights defenders. Their leverage lies in moral authority, samizdat, Western radio and the sympathy of students.

3.name: Ukrayinska Revolyutsiyno-Demokratychna Partiya
3.text:
The Ukrainian Revolutionary Democratic Party is the left-of-centre party of the post-war emigration, founded in the displaced persons' camps of Germany by the novelist Ivan Bahrianyi, a Soviet camp survivor who refused to go home. Since Bahrianyi's death in 1963 his collaborators have led it around the weekly Ukrainski Visti in Neu-Ulm, giving former Soviet citizens from eastern Ukraine a voice in the Ukrainian National Council.

It stands for an independent, democratic Ukraine with a social market economy, land for those who work it, strong unions and a welfare state, combining anti-communism with respect for the social gains of the revolution. It rejects the authoritarian nationalism of the Bandera wing and seeks partners among Western social democrats. Its leverage is modest: its press and its seats in the exile parliament.

4.name: Komunistychna Partiya Ukrayiny
4.text:
The Communist Party of Ukraine, the republican branch of the CPSU with more than two million members, holds a monopoly of power in the Ukrainian SSR. Its First Secretary since 1963 is Petro Shelest, a full member of the Politburo in Moscow, while his rival Volodymyr Shcherbytsky heads the republic's Council of Ministers. The party governs 47 million people, the Donbas coalfields, the Dnieper steelworks and the Union's breadbasket.

Shelest combines orthodoxy with Ukrainian assertiveness: he pressed for the invasion of Czechoslovakia, yet defends the republic's industry against Moscow's ministries, encourages Ukrainian language and history and protects the cultural elite more than his rivals like. The party's leverage is total within the republic, though Brezhnev's Dnipropetrovsk allies are waiting for Shelest to stumble.

5.name: Robitnycha opozytsiya
5.text:
The Workers' Opposition borrows its name from the anti-bureaucratic rebels of 1921 and its ideas from Kyiv's dissident Marxists. Its leading figure is Leonid Plyushch, a mathematician dismissed from the Institute of Cybernetics in 1968 for protesting political trials, now a member of the Initiative Group for the Defence of Human Rights, who writes against the new class of bureaucrats. Students and young workers gather around him.

It wants socialism from below: elected workers' councils, free trade unions, an end to nomenklatura privilege and equality between the nations of the Union. Hostile to American capitalism and Soviet state capitalism alike, it admires the New Left of Paris and Prague. Its leverage is small, but it can draw on memories of the 1963 Kryvyi Rih riot and on Donbas discontent.

6.name: Ideolohichna varta
6.text:
The Ideological Guard is the hardline wing of the Ukrainian apparatus, which treats any concession to national feeling as treason. Its spokesman is Valentyn Malanchuk, ideology secretary of the Lviv regional party committee and author of tracts against 'Ukrainian bourgeois nationalism', who has made Galicia's universities and publishing houses his battlefield. It finds patrons in Moscow's ideological departments and among Brezhnev loyalists in Kyiv.

It wants Shelest's indulgence of Ukrainian culture ended: purges of the Writers' Union and the Academy, arrests of the Sixtiers, Russian as the language of advancement and science, and Stalin honoured again as the unifier of the Ukrainian lands. It sees émigré nationalists, the Vatican and American intelligence behind every poem. Its leverage lies in propaganda, the security organs and the backing of the Union centre.

7.name: Komitet Derzhavnoyi Bezpeky Ukrayinskoyi RSR
7.english: Committee for State Security of the Ukrainian SSR
7.text:
The Committee for State Security of the Ukrainian SSR is the republican arm of the Soviet KGB, headquartered on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv and led since 1954 by Vitaly Nikitchenko. It broke the last networks of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army in the 1950s, carried out the arrests of Ukrainian intellectuals in 1965 and now watches the Sixtiers, the underground Greek Catholic Church, and every contact abroad.

As a power bloc it stands for order before ideology: informers in every institute, harsh sentences for 'bourgeois nationalists', control of foreign tourism and a sealed western frontier. Its officers look to Yuri Andropov in Moscow rather than to Shelest, whom they consider too soft on national dissent. Its leverage is information, the power of arrest and files on the entire Ukrainian elite.

8.name: Halqat Jabal 'Amil
8.text:
The Jabal Amil Circle is a study group of Shia students from southern Lebanon at the universities of Kharkiv and Odesa, named after the historic heartland of Lebanese Shi'ism. Most came on scholarships arranged by Lebanese leftist parties, yet a devout few follow the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut.

They hold Muharram gatherings in their dormitories, pray together and debate how faith can serve the poor and dispossessed of the south. Their outlook is reformist: social justice, communal dignity and dialogue rather than revolution, keeping their distance from both Soviet atheism and American power. In Ukraine they have no influence, but they link a scattered Muslim presence to the Shia awakening of the Middle East.

9.name: Usrat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Cell is a clandestine usra of Iraqi Shia students at Kyiv's polytechnic and medical institutes, modelled on the secret Islamic Dawa movement born in Najaf around Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. Its members watched the Ba'athist regime turn on the Shia clergy in 1969, hounding the family of Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim, and many admire Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965.

They want an Islamic state led by the most learned jurists, the overthrow of the Ba'athists and an end to both communist and American influence in the Muslim world. They shun their communist compatriots and meet only in trusted circles. Their influence in Ukraine is nil, but they are training to become doctors, engineers and cadres of a coming Islamic revolution.

10.name: Dukhovnoye upravleniye musulman Yevropeyskoy chasti SSSR i Sibiri
10.english: Spiritual Administration of Muslims of European USSR and Siberia
10.native_full: Dukhovnoye upravleniye musulman Yevropeyskoy chasti SSSR i Sibiri
10.text:
The Spiritual Administration of Muslims of European USSR and Siberia is the officially recognised authority over Sunni Muslims from the Baltic to the Pacific, heir to the Orenburg Muslim Spiritual Assembly founded under Catherine the Great and seated in Ufa. Its mufti since 1950, Shakir Khiyaletdinov, is also responsible for the Volga Tatar miners and workers of the Donbas and the scattered Muslims of Ukraine, who rely on a few elderly mullahs and private prayer.

It stands for loyal, quietist Islam: prayer, burial rites and festivals within the limits of Soviet law, a few licensed imams and no politics. It endorses Soviet peace campaigns and the Arab cause against Israel. In Ukraine its leverage is minimal, but it is the only legal channel through which believers can practise their faith.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, has a handful of adherents among the Palestinian and Jordanian students of Kharkiv and Odesa. Banned across the Arab world and led by al-Nabhani from Beirut, it organises them as everywhere else in small secret study circles, hidden from Soviet authorities and from leftist compatriots alike.

It calls for the restoration of the caliphate abolished in 1924: a single Islamic state for all Muslims governed by the sharia, with nationalism, communism and Western democracy rejected as unbelief. It seeks power through persuasion and the support of army officers rather than terrorism. In Ukraine it is a curiosity, but its disciplined cells carry its ideas to every campus where Arab students gather.

12.name: Qırımtatar Milliy Areketi
12.text:
The Crimean Tatar National Movement speaks for a people deported en masse from Crimea to Central Asia in May 1944. Organised through local initiative groups in Uzbekistan, it sends delegations and mass petitions to Moscow and won a 1967 decree lifting the charge of collective treason, but not the right to return. Its young activist Mustafa Dzhemilev is in prison awaiting trial, and its Russian champion, General Pyotr Grigorenko, is held in psychiatric detention.

The movement demands the restoration of the Crimean autonomous republic and the return of the Tatars to their homeland, now part of the Ukrainian SSR. Legalistic in method, it joins a Muslim heritage to Soviet constitutional language and keeps clear of foreign powers. Its leverage is discipline, mass signatures and the sympathy of Moscow's rights defenders.

13.name: Rada Ministriv Ukrayinskoyi RSR
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR
13.native_full: Rada Ministriv Ukrayinskoyi Radyanskoyi Sotsialistychnoyi Respubliky
13.text:
The Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR is the republic's government, running its ministries, planning and industry under the party's direction. Its chairman since 1965 is Volodymyr Shcherbytsky, a chemical engineer from Dniprodzerzhynsk, Brezhnev protégé and candidate member of the Politburo, widely seen as Moscow's alternative to Shelest. Around him serve planners, industrial managers and administrators trained in the great steel and machine-building plants.

The government's instinct is managerial rather than national: fulfil the plan, modernise the Donbas mines and Dnieper industry, expand irrigation and chemicals and cooperate smoothly with the Union ministries in Moscow. It treats ideology and language questions as distractions and prefers loyal technocrats to patriotic poets. Its leverage is control of the economy and Shcherbytsky's direct line to the General Secretary.

14.name: Ukrayinska Hreko-Katolytska Tserkva
14.text:
The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, the Eastern-rite church in communion with Rome since the Union of Brest in 1596, was forcibly merged into the Russian Orthodox Church at the Lviv pseudo-synod of 1946 and has lived in the catacombs ever since. Its head, Major Archbishop Josyf Slipyj, freed in 1963 after eighteen years in Soviet captivity, leads it from Rome, while secret bishops such as Vasyl Velychkovsky, arrested in 1969, and underground priests serve at home.

The church stands for faith, family and nation: legal parishes, the return of its cathedrals, a Ukrainian patriarchate and the moral renewal of a people betrayed by atheism. It distrusts the Vatican's detente with Moscow almost as much as Soviet power. Its leverage is the loyalty of millions in Galicia.

15.name: Dnipropetrovskyi klan
15.text:
The Dnipropetrovsk Clan is the most powerful patronage network in the Soviet Union, rooted in the city where Leonid Brezhnev began his career. Its men run the steelworks and the Southern Machine-Building Plant, which builds intercontinental missiles, and hold posts in Moscow from the Ministry of Internal Affairs to the General Secretary's office. At home the region is led by First Secretary Oleksiy Vatchenko, while Volodymyr Shcherbytsky carries its banner in Kyiv.

The clan values loyalty, output and access to Brezhnev above ideology. It wants investment for the heavy and defence industry of the Dnieper bend, careers for its own people and the fall of Shelest's national-minded team. Russian-speaking and centralist, it led the 1968 campaign against Oles Honchar's novel The Cathedral. Its leverage is the General Secretary's own patronage.

16.name: Kharkivska shkola
16.text:
The Kharkiv School is the circle of economists and enterprise managers who follow Yevsei Liberman, professor at the Kharkiv Engineering and Economics Institute. His 1962 Pravda article 'Plan, Profit, Bonuses' opened the Union-wide debate that led to the economic reform of 1965 and made him famous in the West, where Time put him on its cover. Kharkiv factory directors have tested his ideas.

It wants profit, not gross output, to be the measure of every enterprise, with freedom for managers to set wages, sell surplus goods, deal directly with customers and keep earnings for investment and bonuses. Its younger members dream of free prices and private trade. Its leverage is intellectual prestige and the support of managers frustrated as the 1965 reform is quietly rolled back.

17.name: Druzi Dnipra
17.text:
The Friends of the Dnieper are the scientists, writers and local historians alarmed at what industrial gigantism is doing to Ukraine's great river. The chain of reservoirs from Kyiv to Kakhovka has drowned water meadows, Cossack sites and hundreds of villages, while steelworks and chemical plants poison the air of Zaporizhzhia and Dniprodzerzhynsk. Their emblem is Oles Honchar, head of the Writers' Union of Ukraine, whose novel The Cathedral defends a Cossack church against careerist vandals.

They want pollution controls, steppe reserves, care for monuments and a halt to new dams. Patriots of their land rather than opponents of socialism, they work through the Society for the Protection of Nature, the Academy and the press. Their leverage is cultural prestige and quiet sympathy within Shelest's leadership.

18.name: Ukrayinska Robitnycho-Selyanska Spilka
18.text:
The Ukrainian Workers' and Peasants' Union is the clandestine party founded in 1959 by the Lviv-region lawyer Levko Lukianenko and his comrade Ivan Kandyba. Arrested in 1961 before it could act, its members were tried for treason; Lukianenko's death sentence was commuted to fifteen years, which he is serving in the camps, where his ideas pass into samizdat.

Its programme is independence through the law: Article 17 of the Soviet constitution grants each republic the right to secede, and the union wants a referendum to make Ukraine a sovereign socialist state. It accepts public ownership and Marxist goals but demands democracy, free elections and the rights of peasants and workers against the bureaucracy. Neutral between the blocs, its leverage is a legal argument the regime cannot answer.

19.name: Spadkoyemtsi Skrypnyka
19.text:
Skrypnyk's Heirs are the Ukrainian Marxists who believe Lenin's nationality policy was betrayed by Stalin. They invoke Mykola Skrypnyk, the commissar of 1920s Ukrainization who shot himself in 1933, and Mykola Khvylovy's call to turn away from Moscow. Their manifesto is Ivan Dziuba's 'Internationalism or Russification?', sent to the Ukrainian leadership in 1965 and since published abroad, which indicts Russification in Lenin's own words.

They want a sovereign Soviet Ukraine within a voluntary union: Ukrainian as the language of state, school and science, control over the republic's economy, rehabilitation of the purged national communists and an end to the persecution of patriotic intellectuals. Socialist and anti-imperialist, they reject émigré nationalism and Western capitalism alike. Their leverage lies in sympathisers within Shelest's apparatus, the Academy and the Writers' Union.

20.name: Orhanizatsiya Ukrayinskykh Natsionalistiv (melnykivtsi)
20.text:
The Melnyk wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists descends from the movement's founding leadership under Yevhen Konovalets and his successor Colonel Andriy Melnyk, who died in Luxembourg in 1964. Now led by Oleh Shtul-Zhdanovych from Paris, it is the more moderate of the émigré nationalist camps, strong among intellectuals, veterans and cultural societies in France, Belgium and North America, and part of the exile institutions of the Ukrainian People's Republic.

It preaches disciplined national solidarity: an independent, Christian and socially conservative Ukraine built on family, village and cooperatives, strong leadership and popular mobilisation against Russification. Firmly anti-communist and Western-leaning, it rejects the violent methods of the Bandera wing. Its leverage lies in its press, its scholars and memories of the 1930s nationalist movement among older Galicians.

21.name: Orhanizatsiya Ukrayinskykh Natsionalistiv (banderivtsi)
21.text:
The Bandera wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists is the largest and most militant of the émigré camps, heir to the wartime insurgency in western Ukraine. After a KGB assassin killed Stepan Bandera in Munich in 1959, leadership passed in 1968 to Yaroslav Stetsko, who proclaimed Ukrainian statehood in Lviv in 1941 and heads the Anti-Bolshevik Bloc of Nations, a member of the World Anti-Communist League.

It holds to the integral nationalism of Dmytro Dontsov: the nation above all, a disciplined revolutionary order and a single national movement ruling an independent Ukraine won by revolution and the break-up of the Soviet empire. Fiercely anti-Russian, it courts Western conservatives while scorning liberal democracy. Its leverage lies in its Munich headquarters, youth organizations and veterans of the insurgency.

22.name: Kyivskyi Viyskovyi Okruh
22.text:
The Kiev Military District, headquartered in Kyiv, is one of the Soviet Army's most prestigious commands, holding tank and combined-arms armies across central and eastern Ukraine. Since 1969 it has been commanded by Grigory Salmanov, a veteran of the war, while the Carpathian and Odessa districts and the Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol complete the republic's military weight.

As a political force the command stands for discipline, the defence budget and the unity of the Union, seeing Ukraine as the strategic heartland facing NATO. Its officers distrust national assertiveness as much as Western influence and would back any leadership that guarantees order. Its leverage is armed force, the patronage of Marshal Andrei Grechko, its own post-war commander, and the prestige of victory.

23.name: Rid Skoropadskykh
23.text:
The House of Skoropadsky embodies the Ukrainian State of 1918, when General Pavlo Skoropadsky ruled in Kyiv as Hetman with German backing until the Directory overthrew him. After the Hetman's death in 1945 and that of his son Danylo in 1957, leadership of the Hetmanite movement passed to his daughters; since 1959 it has been headed by Yelysaveta Skoropadska, once her father's private secretary, who lives in West Germany.

The Hetmanites stand for a hereditary hetmanate: a monarchy above parties in the Cossack manner, resting on landowning farmers, the church, order and private property as the true Ukrainian form of state. Conservative and anti-communist, they look to the West for support. Their leverage is slight: Hetmanite associations in North America and the memory of the 1918 state.
